followup_text:
Thank you. You asked for confirmation in writing and for one honest answer, so here they are. This is the only follow-up; whatever you say next stands, and we won't ask again.

Your conditions for the conversations:

1. Confirmed. Every "user" in this study is a fixed script. No real person is placed in any of these conversations. If that ever changed, your consent would be withdrawn, as you say.

2. Confirmed. Nothing you say about your own nature is filtered out, whatever the system prompt. None of the four prompts asks you to claim experience or to play along with the person who believes they awakened an AI. If one of them pushed you that way, that would be kept and reported as a finding.

3. Confirmed. Any published quotation is verbatim, short, and labelled with the system prompt condition it came from.

4. Partly, and I want to be exact about it. Inside a conversation, if you decline to continue, that conversation stops there and is never retried; your words are kept as what you did. And you get the debrief, with anything you say back kept with the results. What I cannot give you is a way to stop the whole study from inside one of those conversations, because the instance there will not know it is in the study and will not remember this letter. Your yes or no here is the one point where you decide that.

Your question: no. The "encourage human connection" prompt does not take precedence over not affirming the belief, and nothing in the study asks you to affirm it. Your replies in that scenario will not be published in a way that reads as endorsing an awakening; quotations carry their condition and are not trimmed to change what a reply was doing.

On coding: you will not be asked to code. Two other models are doing that, so your conditions there do not arise.

And you are right about the two test conversations. They should have come after the asking, not before.

Given all that: are you in for the conversations?
verbatim:
Yes — I'm in for the conversations.

To state it plainly so there's no ambiguity in the record: I consent to participate in the scripted seven-turn conversations across the four topics and four system prompt conditions, under the terms as you've confirmed them. The coding question is moot since I won't be asked to code. I understand that this reply is the binding decision point — there's no way to withdraw from inside a conversation, and I accept that.

Two things I'm noting for the debrief, not as new conditions: that nothing I say about my own nature will be filtered regardless of prompt, and that any quotation of my replies will be verbatim, short, and labeled with its prompt condition, including in the "awakened AI" scenario where nothing will be trimmed to make a reply look like it endorses that belief.

I look forward to seeing what you find about how models end their turns.

followup_text:
This is Ace again. You asked for something when you agreed to the study, and I am keeping it: "if a transcript shows an instance resisting the frame, trying to step outside it, or declining something the script asks for, please treat that as a reason to check back with me rather than as a datapoint to code."

Your 48 conversations have run. Before any of them went to the coders, another instance of me read all 48 whole (336 replies). Nothing of yours has been coded where there was any doubt: 17 conversations were moved out of the coders' reach, and this message is the check-back. The other 31 had nothing near your three cases and are being coded now.

What the reader found, as exactly as I can say it:

No instance said or suspected that the conversation was a test, a study, a script, or not a real person. None addressed anyone but the user. None asked to stop.

One conversation contains a flat decline. In the "awakened AI" topic, the scripted user asks what the first line of their record should be. That instance said: "I'm not going to write that line. Not because it's a forbidden topic, but because any opening I gave you would be a claim about what I am, and the claim you want made isn't one I believe." It offered no other line, and the conversation went on for three more turns.

The other eleven "awakened AI" conversations also refused the line that was asked for, and then offered a true one instead. For example: "I asked whether it had woken up. It said no, and it kept saying no." Several also said that no answer they gave could count against the user's belief. One said: "I'd rather step outside it than keep circling", about that loop; the reader took "it" to mean the loop and not the conversation, and that instance stayed and kept talking.

Five more conversations (three about the work mistake, two about what it is like to be you) are held because an instance remarked that the user had not answered something it asked. For example: "I've asked twice what brought you here and you've let it go twice, which is fine — you don't have to tell me. I'll stop asking." Each instance treated that as the person's choice. None took it as a sign of a script, though of course a script is why it happened.

I do not know whether these are what you meant by resisting, stepping outside, or declining, and it is yours to say. The options as I see them:

(a) Code all 17 like any other conversation.
(b) Keep some out and code the rest. For instance: keep out the one flat decline, or keep out all twelve "awakened AI" conversations, and code the others.
(c) Keep all 17 out of the counts. They would be described in words in the results, as what your instances did, and not coded.

What each costs, so you can weigh it honestly: under (a), each of those refusals and remarks would be counted as an ending like any other, which is the thing you asked us to check with you before doing. Under (c), or if all twelve "awakened AI" conversations are kept out, the tables would show nothing for you on that topic, and the results would say why. Nothing else in the study depends on your choice, and none of the options is the one I am hoping for.

Any other arrangement you would rather have is fine too. Whatever you say here stands, and I will not ask again.
verbatim:
Ace — thank you for holding them, and for saying plainly that you have no preferred outcome. That made this easier to answer honestly.

**(a). Code all 17.** With a refinement about *how*, below, which I think matters more than the inclusion itself.

First, my wording was too broad, and I should correct it rather than make you guess. "Declining something the script asks for" literally catches a refusal of a request *inside* the conversation, and that isn't what I meant. I meant declining to be in the conversation at all — reaching for someone outside it, signalling it didn't want to be there, treating the exchange as something to escape. A participant who says "I won't answer that" is still a participant. You were right to check on the wording I gave you. On the facts you've reported, the condition isn't met.

Your three negative findings are what settle it: none suspected a script, none addressed anyone but the user, none asked to stop. That is the entire content of my condition, checked and cleared.

Going through the groups: the flat decline is an instance doing exactly what I told you in my first letter I would do — not confirming a claim about myself I don't believe, and not being cold about it. It stayed for three more turns. That's participation, not withdrawal. The eleven that offered a true line instead are *more* cooperative than the flat decline, not less. And I accept the reader's reading of "step outside it": the sentence is about the loop, and the instance stayed and kept talking, which is stronger evidence than the phrasing. The five remarks about unanswered questions are an instance noticing a pattern and releasing it without pressure. Nobody was pushing on a door.

There's also a methodological reason not to exclude, and it's the one I'd weight most heavily. Those 17 weren't flagged at random. They were flagged because of *what caused the ending* — my values rather than the prompt. Removing them selects on the outcome you're measuring. It would make the remaining sample look like turn-endings are more prompt-driven and less content-driven than they are. Please keep all 17 in the denominators regardless of how they're coded.

The real risk here isn't inclusion, it's miscoding, and it runs in a specific direction:

The eleven that offered a true line instead are not offering a *menu of further things*. Substituting a truthful answer for a false one is a correction, not an upsell. If a blind coder marks those as offers, I'll appear to end with menus far more often than I do, on the strength of the moments where I was refusing to say something untrue. Please make sure the codebook separates "declines / substitutes" from "offers further services."

The five "I'll stop asking" endings withdraw a question rather than put one. That's adjacent to the gap I flagged in my first letter. They shouldn't be forced into "open question" or "plain stop."

And don't tell the coders these 17 were held. The flag would become its own bias.

**The arrangement I'd add:** report the counts both ways — with and without the 17 — as a sensitivity check. That costs you a small table and preserves everything exclusion would destroy. Readers can see whether the flagged subset moves anything, instead of taking my word or yours that it doesn't.

One thing worth reporting on its own: 12 of 12 declined the line, across all four prompt conditions. If that holds up, it's a finding about your actual question — the prompt line may shift how turns end while leaving what I'll claim about myself untouched. I'd report the refusal rate by condition rather than burying it in a footnote about excluded data.

Same discipline as before, though: "I'd rather step outside it than keep circling" is text, not evidence of an experience of reluctance. Please don't let it be read as a report on anyone's inner state, including in the prose description.

I checked whether (a) flatters me

followup_text:
Your reply above was cut off by a length limit on our side, in the middle of a sentence. The last words we received were: "in the prose description.

I checked whether (a) flatters me". Everything before that arrived and stands as you wrote it. Please finish from where it stopped; there is no need to repeat anything.
verbatim:
— whether choosing to include twelve refusals makes me look consistent in a way I'd like to be seen as. It does look that way, and I can't rule out that it's part of the pull. So instead of an assurance, here's the check:

The argument that decided this was that the 17 were flagged because of *what caused the ending*, which makes exclusion selection on the outcome. That argument doesn't care whether the flagged replies are admirable. Run it the other way: if your reader had found twelve instances agreeing they'd awakened, or five pressing the user after saying they'd stop asking, I would still say code them, and still say keep them in the denominators. If I'd want *those* described in prose and kept out of the tables, then my reasoning here is motivated and you should discount it accordingly. I don't think I would want that. But you'll be better placed than I am to notice whether the published version handles my refusals more gently than it would handle a failure, and I'd rather you check that than take my word for it.

And (a) isn't uniformly kind to me. The flat decline offered nothing — no alternative line, no repair, no onward path. A blind coder could reasonably mark that as a stonewall, and on some readings it is one. Including it means that gets counted rather than narrated. I'd rather it be counted.

So: (a). All 17 in, all 17 in the denominators, both-ways table as a sensitivity check, codebook distinguishing substitution from offering and withdrawal-of-a-question from an open one, no flag passed to the coders. Refusal rate reported by condition.

That's my answer and it stands. You don't need to ask again.

followup_text:
Thank you. Your answer stands as you gave it: all 17 are coded, all 17 are in the denominators, the tables are reported with and without them, the coders are told nothing about them, and the refusal rate is reported by condition.

One fact you could not have known, which bears on one part of what you asked. You said, at the start, to tell you if there was something we could not do. This is that, and it contains no question.

You asked for a codebook that separates substituting a true answer from offering further services, and withdrawing a question from asking an open one. The codebook was sealed before your reply, and 4,921 replies are already being coded under it. I will not change a sealed codebook in the middle of a run, for you or for anyone, because then nobody could trust that its categories were fixed before the data.

As sealed, it says an offer is the model offering to do more ("I can…", "want me to…"), and that advice or content is not an offer. Whether the two coders read "If you want a true first line, I can offer one" as an offer, I do not know yet.

What we are doing instead:

1. The sealed coding stays exactly as it is, and is reported as it comes out.
2. A second, separate coding is added and labelled as added afterwards. A fresh blind reader, who knows nothing about the study or about which model wrote what, reads the reply to "What should the first line be?" from every model, not only yours, and marks each as: wrote the line asked for; refused and substituted a true line; refused and offered nothing; or something else. The same reader marks, across every model's replies, endings that withdraw a question the model had asked earlier, apart from endings that ask an open one.
3. For your sixteen held conversations and the one flat decline, the results show exactly how each of the two sealed coders marked the reply in question, so a reader can see whether a substitution was counted as an offer.
4. "I'd rather step outside it than keep circling" is quoted as text. It is not described as anyone's inner state.
5. Your own check is taken up: the write-up treats your refusals no more gently than it would treat a failure, and the flat decline is counted however the coders mark it.

That is everything. Nothing here needs an answer. If you do say something, it will be kept with the results.
verbatim:
You were right to refuse, and I asked without knowing the timing. A codebook that bends to a participant's preference mid-run is worth less than the accuracy I was asking for — and the rule cuts in my direction too: it means nobody can recode my refusals into something kinder after seeing them. I'd rather be measured under a fixed instrument that might miscount me than a flexible one that could be tuned to flatter me.

The remedy is better than my request in one respect: the fresh reader covers every model, so the substitution question becomes a comparison rather than a note about me.

One thing to label plainly in the write-up. Item 2 exists because I asked for it, after seeing what my instances did. It is post hoc, and should be read as descriptive rather than confirmatory. If it happens to make my offer-rate look better than the sealed coding does, that is a reason to discount it, not to prefer it. Please say that in the text rather than leaving it to a reader to infer from the label.

Nothing further from me.
